questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

Tests CRD API access from a pod, ConfigMap-driven runtime configuration, Secret-based credentials, InitContainer usage, and proper observability with probes and PVC-backed logs. It also touches network isolation via NetworkPolicy in a CKAD-appropriate setting.

## Key Concepts

- CRD watch and API access from a namespace-scoped Pod
- ConfigMap as dynamic WINDOW configuration
- Secret-stored Bearer token for outbound POST
- InitContainer for tooling installation
- Readiness/Liveness probes for a long-running auditor
- Logs persisted to a PVC
- Namespace NetworkPolicy restricting egress

## Code Example

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
data:
  audit-config: |
    window: 60
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
data:
  audit-token: <base64-encoded-token>
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: crd-auditor
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: crd-auditor
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: crd-auditor
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: crd-auditor-sa
      initContainers:
      - name: install-tools
        image: alpine:3.18
        command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache curl jq"]
        volumeMounts:
        - mountPath: /logs
          name: logs
      containers:
      - name: auditor
        image: my-registry/crd-auditor:latest
        env:
        - name: AUDIT_CONFIG
          valueFrom:
            configMapKeyRef:
              name: audit-config
              key: window
        - name: AUDIT_TOKEN
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: audit-token
              key: token
        volumeMounts:
        - mountPath: /logs
          name: logs
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 15
          periodSeconds: 20
      volumes:
      - name: logs
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: crd-auditor-logs
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you simulate CRD changes locally for tests?
- How would you handle CRD API version upgrades and backward compatibility?

## Why This Is Asked

Evaluates CKAD fundamentals: ConfigMap/Secret usage, zero-downtime rolling updates, and health checks.

## Key Concepts

- ConfigMap vs Secret usage
- envFrom vs volumeMounts
- Readiness/Liveness probes
- RollingUpdate strategy
- Resource requests/limits

## Code Example

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: app-config
data:
  APP_PORT: 8080
  LOG_LEVEL: info

---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: app-secrets
stringData:
  DB_PASSWORD: mypassword

---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  replicas: 3
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxUnavailable: 0
      maxSurge: 1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: api
    spec:

          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 8080

          httpGet:
```

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical hardening: container securityContext, readiness/liveness, graceful shutdown, high-availability with PDB, and network isolation via NetworkPolicy.

## Key Concepts
- Pod securityContext and container securityContext
- Probes and lifecycle hooks
- PodDisruptionBudget
- NetworkPolicy basics and egress constraints
- Per-namespace isolation in production-grade CKAD

## Code Example
```javascript
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api
  namespace: secure
spec:
  replicas: 2
  template:
    spec:
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: api:latest
        securityContext:
          runAsUser: 10001
          readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
          allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
          capabilities:
            drop: ["ALL"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: config
          mountPath: /etc/api-config
        - name: secret
          mountPath: /etc/api-secret
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "100m"
            memory: "128Mi"
          limits:
            cpu: "500m"
            memory: "512Mi"
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /readyz
            port: 8080
        lifecycle:
          preStop:
            exec:
              command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "sleep 5"]
      volumes:
      - name: config
        configMap:
          name: api-config
      - name: secret
        secret:
          secretName: api-secret
---
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: api-pdb
  namespace: secure
spec:
  minAvailable: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: api-egress
  namespace: secure
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
      ipBlock:
        cidr: 10.96.0.0/12
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 443
  - to:
      namespaceSelector: {}
    ports:
    - protocol: UDP
      port: 53
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you monitor and validate performance under load?
- How would you rollback the namespace isolation changes safely?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This question tests practical CKAD skills, including permissioning, automation, and Kubernetes-native policy enforcement using a CronJob with ConfigMap-driven behavior.

## Key Concepts
- Namespace-scoped CronJob for periodic enforcement
- ConfigMap-driven policy configuration (imageRepo, imageTag)
- kubectl patch or server-side apply for image updates
- PVC-based logging and HTTP POST for audit trails
- InitContainer for tooling installation (curl, jq)
- Namespace NetworkPolicy scoping for egress control

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: image-tag-enforcer
  namespace: default
spec:
  schedule: "*/5 * * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          initContainers:
          - name: installer
            image: busybox
            command: ["sh", "-c", "apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl jq"]
          containers:
          - name: enforcer
            image: curlimages/curl:latest
            command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
            args:
            - |
              # Read policy from ConfigMap
              # Get all Deployments in namespace
              # Compare images against policy
              # Patch mismatched Deployments
              # Write heartbeat log to /logs
              # POST summary to policy-portal
            volumeMounts:
            - name: log-volume
              mountPath: /logs
            readinessProbe:
              exec:
                command: ["test", "-f", "/logs/ready"]
              initialDelaySeconds: 5
              periodSeconds: 10
            livenessProbe:
              exec:
                command: ["test", "-f", "/logs/alive"]
              initialDelaySeconds: 15
              periodSeconds: 20
          volumes:
          - name: log-volume
            persistentVolumeClaim:
              claimName: enforcer-logs
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: restrict-egress
  namespace: default
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: policy-portal
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 8080
```

## Trade-offs
- **Frequency**: Running every 5 minutes balances responsiveness vs. resource usage; longer intervals reduce API load but delay remediation
- **PVC vs. Sidecar**: Using a PVC is simpler but requires storage provisioning; a sidecar could stream logs directly
- **Patch vs. Reconcile Controller**: A declarative controller would be more robust but requires custom operator development; CronJob is quicker to implement but imperative
- **InitContainer**: Pre-installing tools increases pod startup time; consider using a custom image with tools baked in instead
- **NetworkPolicy**: Restricting egress improves security but may break legitimate communication; ensure all required endpoints are explicitly allowed

## Why This Is Asked
Tests understanding of InitContainer lifecycle, idempotent seeding patterns, and persistent cache management across pod restarts.

## Key Concepts
- InitContainers and startup ordering
- ConfigMap-based seed script injection
- PVC-backed shared cache for idempotence
- Marker file pattern for preventing re-seeding
- Readiness and liveness probe configuration
- Load testing and rollback strategies

## Code Example
```yaml
# Seed script ConfigMap
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: seed-scripts
data:
  seed.sh: |
    #!/bin/sh
    set -e
    if [ ! -f /cache/.seeded ]; then
      # Execute seeding logic here
      touch /cache/.seeded
    fi
---
# Deployment with InitContainer
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api-server
  namespace: ckad
spec:
  replicas: 3
  template:
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: seed-cache
        image: busybox:1.35
        command: ['/bin/sh', '/scripts/seed.sh']
        volumeMounts:
        - name: seed-scripts
          mountPath: /scripts
        - name: cache-volume
          mountPath: /cache
      containers:
      - name: api-server
        image: api-server:latest
        volumeMounts:
        - name: cache-volume
          mountPath: /cache
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 15
          periodSeconds: 20
      volumes:
      - name: seed-scripts
        configMap:
          name: seed-scripts
      - name: cache-volume
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: cache-pvc
```

## Verification Strategy
1. **Load Testing**: Use kubectl exec to simulate concurrent requests, monitor cache seeding behavior, and verify marker file prevents re-seeding
2. **Rollback Approach**: Deploy with strategy type RollingUpdate, set maxUnavailable and maxSurge for controlled rollout, and use kubectl rollout undo if issues arise
3. **Monitoring**: Check InitContainer logs, verify probe status, and confirm cache persistence across pod restarts

## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to design production-ready batch workloads in Kubernetes, including secure configuration management, job lifecycle controls, and deployment strategies for config-driven restarts.

## Key Concepts
- **concurrencyPolicy: Forbid** - Prevents overlapping job executions, ensuring data consistency
- **backoffLimit: 3** - Limits retry attempts for failed pods before marking the job as failed
- **ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 86400** - Auto-cleansup completed jobs after 24 hours
- **successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 3** - Retains recent successful job history for debugging/auditing
- **checksum annotation** - Triggers pod recreation when ConfigMap/Secret changes (requires script to generate hash)
- **envFrom** - Mounts all ConfigMap/Secret values as environment variables without explicit key mapping

## Verification Under Simulated Load
1. **Test concurrency**: Trigger manual job while another runs - should fail with "Cannot determine if job needs to be started"
2. **Test failure handling**: Set invalid config, verify backoff retries 3 times
3. **Test cleanup**: Check completed jobs are removed after 24h TTL

## Verification On Config Change
1. Update ConfigMap: `kubectl apply -f analytics-config.yaml`
2. Verify annotation checksum updates in next job
3. Confirm new pod picks up new environment variables
4. Use `kubectl get pods` to verify new pod creation timestamp

## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to coordinate InitContainers, sidecars, and config-driven apps in CKAD. Ensures proper volume mounting, file-based reloading semantics, and safe network posture.

## Key Concepts
- InitContainer: pre-flight yamllint validation of /configs
- Config mounting: PVC-backed /configs shared with main container and sidecar
- Sidecar watcher: detects changes and triggers in-app reload via /reload/trigger
- Readiness/Liveness probes: ensure proper pod health
- Namespace NetworkPolicy: restricts egress to internal services only

## Code Example
```yaml
# minimal skeleton (Deployment)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: config-reloader
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: config-reloader
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: lint-configs
        image: busybox
        command: ["sh", "-c", "yamllint /configs/**/*.yaml || exit 1"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: config-volume
          mountPath: /configs
      containers:
      - name: main-app
        image: myapp:latest
        volumeMounts:
        - name: config-volume
          mountPath: /configs
        - name: reload-volume
          mountPath: /reload
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 15
          periodSeconds: 20
        env:
        - name: RELOAD_PATH
          value: /reload/trigger
      - name: reload-watcher
        image: alpine:latest
        command: ["sh", "-c", "inotifywait -m /configs -e modify,create -e moved_to | while read; do touch /reload/trigger; done"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: config-volume
          mountPath: /configs
        - name: reload-volume
          mountPath: /reload
      volumes:
      - name: config-volume
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: config-pvc
      - name: reload-volume
        emptyDir: {}
```

## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical CKAD skills: Deployments, ConfigMaps, resources, probes, and autoscaling with verification.

## Key Concepts
- Deployment, ConfigMap, resources, probes, HPA
- Rollout verification, kubectl, metrics-server
- Safe rollout strategies

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web-app
spec:
  replicas: 3
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web-app
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web
        image: nginx:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
        envFrom:
        - configMapRef:
            name: web-env
        resources:
          requests:
            memory: "128Mi"
            cpu: "100m"
          limits:
            memory: "256Mi"
            cpu: "250m"
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /
            port: 80
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /
            port: 80
          initialDelaySeconds: 15
          periodSeconds: 20
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you adapt this for a multi-tenant cluster? 
- What changes if the app uses a sidecar log collector?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to coordinate InitContainers with main containers, use ConfigMap/Secret mounted data, and implement health checks for reliable startups.

## Key Concepts
- InitContainers sequencing
- ConfigMap/Secret mounts
- Probes for startup health
- Rollback and load testing

## Code Example
```yaml
# fragment patch adding initContainer and volumes
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: stock-service
  namespace: inventory
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: seed-db
        image: postgres:15
        command:
        - bash
        - -lc
        - until pg_isready -h postgresql.inventory.svc -p 5432; do sleep 2; done; psql -h postgresql.inventory.svc -U dbuser -d inventory -f /seed/init.sql
        env:
        - name: PGPASSWORD
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: db-credentials
              key: password
        volumeMounts:
        - name: seed-files
          mountPath: /seed
      containers:
      - name: stock-service
        image: my-reg/stock-service:latest
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 8080
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 8080
      volumes:
      - name: seed-files
        configMap:
          name: stock-seed-config
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you ensure idempotent seeds across restarts?
- How would you scale this pattern for multiple environments?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests CKAD proficiency across namespace-scoped automation, ConfigMap manipulation, InitContainers, and secure egress controls in real-world migration workflows.

## Key Concepts
- CronJob scoped to a namespace with per-namespace behavior
- InitContainer to install tooling (yq) and prepare environment
- ConfigMap-driven migration plan and idempotent updates
- PVC-backed logs and a Secret-backed external POST
- Readiness/Liveness probes for resilient Jobs
- Namespace NetworkPolicy to restrict egress to the migration portal

## Code Example
```yaml
# Minimal skeleton: per-namespace CronJob migrating ConfigMaps
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: config-migrate
  namespace: target-namespace
spec:
  schedule: "0 * * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          serviceAccountName: migrate-sa
          initContainers:
          - name: installer
            image: alpine:3.17
            command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache go && go install github.com/mikefarah/yq@latest"]
          containers:
          - name: migrate
            image: my-registry/config-migrate:latest
            envFrom:
            - secretRef:
                name: migration-api
            volumeMounts:
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /logs
            readinessProbe:
              httpGet:
                path: /healthz
                port: 8080
              initialDelaySeconds: 5
              periodSeconds: 10
            livenessProbe:
              httpGet:
                path: /healthz
                port: 8080
              initialDelaySeconds: 15
              periodSeconds: 20
          volumes:
          - name: logs
            persistentVolumeClaim:
              claimName: logs-pvc
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you ensure idempotent migrations across runs?
- How would you handle partial failures or large numbers of ConfigMaps?
- What monitoring would you add to detect drift or failures?
